slide.heading: Stroke
slide.subheading: Time is brain: vascular territories and the first hour

lines.text: Stroke. In a large ischemic stroke, the brain loses nearly two million neurons for every minute the artery stays blocked.
Most strokes are ischemic: a clot, from a diseased artery or thrown from the heart. The rest are bleeds.
Your job in the first hour is to recognize it, localize it, and get the patient to treatment. Every minute counts.

slide.heading: BE-FAST
bullets: Balance: sudden loss of coordination
Eyes: sudden loss of vision
Face: one side droops
Arm (or leg): one side weak
Speech, and Time: note when last known well

lines.text: The public learns BE-FAST: balance, eyes, face, arm, speech, and time.
The most important question you'll ask is when the patient was last known to be well. Not when the symptoms were found: when they were last seen normal.

slide.heading: Where is the stroke?
bullets: MCA: face and arm more than leg, opposite side
Left (dominant) MCA: aphasia
Right MCA: neglect of the left side
ACA: leg more than arm
PCA: homonymous hemianopia (macula spared)

rows: Aphasia (dominant) or neglect; gaze toward lesion

lines.text: The homunculus predicts the territories. The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral cortex: the face and arm areas. Block it and the opposite face and arm are weaker than the leg.
In the dominant hemisphere, usually the left, it also takes language: aphasia. On the right, the patient may ignore the left side of the world.
The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface, where the leg lives: leg weaker than arm.
And the posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe: a homonymous hemianopia, often sparing the center of vision.

slide.heading: The first hour
bullets: Check glucose: hypoglycemia can mimic stroke
Non-contrast CT first: rule out bleeding
IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of last known well
Thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion (up to 24 h if selected)
No thrombolysis if there is hemorrhage

lines.text: Check the glucose: low sugar can look exactly like a stroke.
Then a non-contrast CT of the head, straight away. It's fast, and its main job is to show whether there's blood, because clot-busting drugs would make a bleed worse.
If there's no bleed and the patient is eligible, intravenous thrombolysis can be given within four and a half hours of last known well.
For a large artery blocked by clot, a thrombectomy pulls it out through a catheter, in selected patients up to twenty-four hours out.

slide.heading: Preventing the next stroke
bullets: Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation
Otherwise, antiplatelet therapy
Statin, blood pressure control, stop smoking
Severe symptomatic carotid stenosis: endarterectomy

lines.text: After the acute stroke, find the cause and prevent the next one.
If the heart is throwing clots, as in atrial fibrillation, patients need an anticoagulant, not just aspirin.
Everyone else: an antiplatelet, a statin, blood pressure control and no smoking; and a tight carotid stenosis on the stroke's side may need surgery.

slide.heading: Summary
bullets: Last known well starts the clock
MCA: face and arm; ACA: leg; PCA: vision
CT first, then thrombolysis within 4.5 h
Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulate

lines.text: This afternoon: a patient with sudden weakness in the Clinical Skills Center. Localize it, and don't forget the clock.
